text.p: Tiger Woods followed a superb front nine with a fabulous finish as he charged into contention with a third-round course record-equalling 64 in the British Open on Saturday.

After being tamed by Royal Troon for two days, the Masters champion and world number one reversed roles and conquered the 7,079-yard course for the first time to vault on to the fringe of contention on three under par.
That left the 21-year-old American six shots behind the nine-under par of leader Darren Clarke of Northern Ireland, who had not begun his round when Woods finished.
Woods's round matched the Royal Troon Open course record of 64 set by Greg Norman in the final round in 1989 and was one outside the Open record of 63 achieved seven times.

Woods negotiated the tough back nine in 32, three under par, including an eagle three at the 542-yard 16th with a 15-footer and a spectacular holed chip shot from down a bank for birdie at the short 16th.
His three-iron tee shot there finished down a bank but he bumped his second shot into the side of the bank to kill its pace and watched as it rolled on to the green and curled into the cup.
Then he saved par from a greenside bunker at the last.
Earlier Woods had made a par four at the 10th, where he had quadruple bogey eight on Friday, but then flirted with disaster at the same 11th hole where he took a triple bogey seven on Thursday.
This time, after driving into gorse and taking two shots to escape, he got away with a bogey five.
He birdied the 12th from five feet.
"The bogey at 11 kept me going because it could have been much worse," he said. "I played the bump and run at the 17th because I prefer it to a lob shot."
"It's up to the leaders how far behind I am at the end of the day. They are in control because the wind is not blowing," he said.
"I can go lower. I had two bogeys today. But I'm hitting my irons very sharp. I just have to eliminate the bogeys."
Woods started out 13 shots behind leader Clarke after rounds of 72 and 74 and quickly took advantage of the perfect scoring conditions he failed to exploit on Friday.
His pitch to the first green ended two feet from the pin for a birdie and he rammed in a monster 40-footer at the second.
He got up and down after missing the third green for par and reached the long par-five fourth green in two and two-putted from 40 feet for his third birdie.
The short fifth cost Woods his only bogey of the front nine when he missed the green and after chipping missed an eight-foot par putt.
Then he almost eagled the long sixth from 15 feet but had to settle for birdie.
His off-line drive at the 402-yard seventh hit a girl in the crowd and deflected on to the fairway, from where he pitched to 10 feet and holed for yet another birdie.

Woods struck his tee shot at the Postage Stamp eighth to 12 feet and missed the birdie putt, then just missed a 50-foot birdie attempt at nine before holing his return four-footer to complete his outgoing nine of 32.
After his par at 10, Woods drove left into thick gorse at the 463-yard 11th. He donned his waterproof suit and ventured into the jungle but could only advance his ball into more gorse.
But he put his third shot to the edge of the fairway, almost hit the flag with a 50-yard pitch and holed from three feet to get away with a five.
Veteran American Jack Nicklaus did the best of the earliest starters playing in the first group with compatriot Payne Stewart of the 70 who survived the halfway cut.
Nicklaus birdied the fourth and fifth holes and eagled the 577-yard sixth after a one-iron second to 30 feet and a fine putt.
Then he gave all his gains back with five bogeys on the back nine before a birdie at the last finished off a level-par round of 71.
"I had an opportunity if I played a good back nine to move up in the golf tournament," Nicklaus, the three-times champion, said.
"After 45 holes without much wind if I happened to shoot a couple under you never know what might happen.
"After playing the back nine in around par for two days, I squandered it with a 39 in easy conditions."
The leaders, Clarke playing with second-placed American Justin Leonard, went off at 1405 GMT.
